newsitem.title: DENMARK: Clinton says Republican tax plan a "time bomb".
newsitem.headline: Clinton says Republican tax plan a "time bomb".

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton on Saturday said Republican congressional tax legislation contains some "time bomb tax cuts" that risk exploding the size of the U.S. deficit in the years ahead.

Clinton, who plans on Tuesday to meet at the White House with Republican and Democratic congressional leaders to discuss the status of the tax and spending cut legislation, used his weekly radio address to warn there was "a right way and a wrong way to cut taxes."

Speaking from Denmark on the last day of an eight-day trip to Europe, Clinton said he hoped to be able to work with congressional Republicans to overcome their differences and craft legislation that honours an agreement with them to balance the federal budget by the year 2002.

The lawmakers will try to carve one final tax bill from the different versions passed by the House and Senate, with an eye to objections raised by the White House over provisions in both. They aimed to present the legislation to the full House and Senate for a vote before the August recess.
The tax bill would turn into law part of a five-year balanced budget agreement between congressional leaders and the White House that called for $85 billion in net tax cuts.
"Unfortunately, the tax plan recommended by the Congress offers too little relief to the middle class and fails to live up to the budget agreement," Clinton said.
"The congressional plan would deny seven million students tuition tax credits," Clinton said and failed to adequately encourage provisions to encourage college or graduate school or career training.
"My tax cut will keep the budget balanced," he said, but tucked away in the congressional plan are time bomb tax cuts that risk exploding the deficit in years to come."
He said a final tax bill "must be fair, giving middle class families the help they need to raise their children, send them to college, buy and sell a home."
"It must not contain provisions which will lead to big budget deficits in years to come," he declared. "This is the kind of tax cut I'm coming home to work with Congress to pass."
"If we stand firm for the right principles, if we stick to a strategy that has secured our prosperity -- invest and grow - - we can prepare our people for the bright new century ahead," Clinton said.
The task of trying to find spending cuts and give tax breaks may have become easier for Clinton and the lawmkers.

Sen. Daniel Moynihan said in Washington on Friday that the Congressional Budget office has slashed its estimate of the federal budget deficit for the current fiscal year ending on September 30 to below $50 billion, down from $67 billion forecast by CBO just two months ago.
The CBO earlier this year had predicted the deficit would be as much as $124 billion.
